summary: Peggy Karp proposes rules for forming ARPANET host names after feedback on her first list in RFC 226. Names would be eight characters, of the form site, dash, machine, with the site part built from the name or a standard acronym. It replaced RFC 226.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo proposes host names built from a site code and a machine code separated by a hyphen. It also describes special codes, alternate names and a way to relate names to network addresses.

subtitle: A proposal for forming host names from short site and machine mnemonics.

tldr.problem: The earlier host-name list was only a starting proposal, and the network needed general rules for forming names.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed name combines a site mnemonic, a hyphen and a machine mnemonic, each limited to four characters.
tldr.outcome: The rules and list remained subject to Network Working Group approval; RFC 247 obsoletes RFC 226.

today: RFC 247 obsoletes RFC 226. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 247.

sections.title: The Site and Machine Name Parts
sections.content:
A host name is eight characters long in the form <site>-<machine>. The site part is at most four characters: use a short site keyword, standard acronym or abbreviation when available, otherwise use the first four letters or a mnemonic chosen by the site's technical liaison.

The machine part is at most four characters and combines a manufacturer number with a designator when multiple machines of the same type are at a site. The memo notes that the four-character limit cannot distinguish every machine with a four-digit manufacturer number, leaving that case for ad hoc handling by the Network Information Center.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose a short code for the site, add a hyphen, then add a short code for the machine. A designator can distinguish machines of the same type at one site.

sections.title: Special Names and Alternate Names
sections.content: Terminal Interface Processors are identified as TIP rather than by the number 316. A host that is not permanently addressable uses TEST as its machine name. The memo asks sites to provide alternate host names as suggested by RFC 236; the technical liaison selects the site's alternate and sends it to the NIC.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo reserves TIP for terminal interface processors and TEST for hosts that are not permanently addressable. Sites can also choose alternate names.

sections.title: A Proposed Address Mapping
sections.content:
An implementation idea attributed to Steve Crocker maps the site to an 8-bit number S and the machine to an 8-bit number M, with S + M = Network Address. The values can be chosen so that naming the site alone defaults to its primary host. The RFC gives examples for UCLA and BBN.

The rules and attached host list are subject to approval by the Network Working Group. The NIC would maintain the list with help from each site's technical liaison.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo sketches a way to combine a site number and machine number into a network address. The proposal still needed approval, and the NIC would maintain the list with each site's liaison.
